technical.prompt: What is corporate venture capital?
expectedPoints: A corporation investing directly in outside startups
Seeks both financial and strategic returns
Often run through a dedicated unit or fund

choices.answer: A corporation investing in outside startups for financial and strategic gains
distractors: A startup investing in large corporations
A bank lending to corporate clients
A company buying back its own shares

technical.prompt: How do strategic returns differ from financial returns in corporate venture capital?
expectedPoints: Financial returns come from the stake's value increasing
Strategic returns include access to technology, partnerships and market insight
Balancing the two is a core challenge

choices.answer: Financial returns are gains; strategic ones benefit the parent
distractors: Strategic returns are always paid as cash dividends
Financial returns come only from partnerships
The two kinds of return are identical in every case

technical.prompt: Why do corporations set up venture arms?

choices.answer: To see new technology early and build partnership or acquisition options
distractors: To avoid paying corporate income tax on profits
To replace their own research and development teams
To lend money to startups at high interest rates

technical.prompt: Why might a startup accept money from a corporate investor?
expectedPoints: Access to customers, distribution or expertise

distractors: Corporate investors never take equity
Corporate money comes with no conditions
Corporate investors guarantee an IPO

technical.prompt: What risks does a startup face when taking corporate venture money?

choices.answer: Rivals of the parent may avoid it, and priorities can change
distractors: It can never raise from other investors
It must merge with the parent
It loses its founders immediately

technical.prompt: What is signalling risk from a corporate investor?

choices.answer: Others may read the corporate's decisions as signals about the startup
distractors: Risk that the startup's phone signal fails
Risk that the corporate's share price falls
Risk that advertising doesn't reach customers

technical.prompt: What is an evergreen corporate venture fund?
expectedPoints: Funded from the parent's balance sheet

choices.answer: A venture arm funded from the parent's balance sheet with no fixed end
distractors: A fund that invests only in agriculture
A fund raised from outside investors with a ten-year life

technical.prompt: Who usually approves investments at a corporate venture arm?

choices.answer: A committee often including senior company executives
distractors: The founders of the startup being funded
The parent company's external auditors

technical.prompt: Why do corporate investments often come with commercial agreements?

Deliver strategic value to the parent
Give the startup revenue and validation

choices.answer: They create strategic value alongside the investment
distractors: They are required before any investment

choices.answer: They give close knowledge of potential acquisition targets
distractors: They force startups to sell to the parent
They replace all acquisitions

technical.prompt: What is a right of first refusal on a sale of the company?

A softer version is a right of first notice

choices.answer: The right to match any offer to buy the company
distractors: The right to refuse to invest again
The right to reject new employees
The right to cancel customer contracts

technical.prompt: Why do information rights create tension for corporate investors?

choices.answer: Startups fear sensitive information could reach a competing parent
distractors: Corporates legally can't receive any information
Startups must share everything publicly
Information rights have no value

technical.prompt: When does a corporation typically use the equity method for a startup investment?

choices.answer: With significant influence, often about 20% to 50% ownership
distractors: Only when it owns more than 90% of the startup
Only when it owns less than 1% of the startup
Only when the startup has become profitable

technical.prompt: How are corporate venture teams often paid compared with independent venture capitalists?

choices.answer: Mostly salary and bonus, often without carried interest
distractors: Entirely through carried interest
Only in the startups' shares
Paid by the startups directly

technical.prompt: Why do corporate venture arms often invest alongside independent venture funds?

Keeps the corporate in a supporting role

choices.answer: Independent funds lead and price rounds, validating the deal
distractors: Independent funds are required by law
Corporates can't write checks alone

technical.prompt: Why can corporate venture arms be less stable than independent funds?

choices.answer: Their budgets and priorities depend on the parent company
distractors: They are funded by thousands of small investors
They must close every ten years

technical.prompt: Why might corporate investors be willing to pay higher valuations?

choices.answer: They value strategic benefits beyond financial return
distractors: They are required to pay double

technical.prompt: How can corporate venture performance be measured?
expectedPoints: Financial returns such as IRR and multiple
Strategic outcomes such as partnerships or technology adopted

choices.answer: By combining financial returns with strategic outcomes
distractors: By financial returns alone, ignoring strategy
By the number of startups met each year
By the size of the venture team's budget

technical.prompt: Why do some corporate venture arms seek independence from business units?

choices.answer: For faster decisions and credibility with founders
distractors: To avoid paying any taxes
To stop reporting to the parent at all

A $5M loss in its income statement

choices.answer: A $5 million loss
distractors: A $20 million loss
No entry until the stake is sold

distractors: A $20 million gain

choices.answer: About $30 million
distractors: About $10 million

technical.prompt: A corporate investor decides not to join a startup's next round. What problems can that cause, and how can it reduce them?
expectedPoints: Other investors may assume negative information
Explain reasons such as strategic shifts

choices.answer: Others may assume bad news; clear communication reduces the damage
distractors: The startup is automatically acquired
Nothing, since corporate decisions are private

technical.prompt: Why do startups and independent investors resist giving a corporate investor a right of first refusal on a sale?

technical.prompt: What are the trade-offs of taking a board seat versus an observer seat for a corporate investor?

Board seats carry no legal duties to the startup

technical.prompt: A corporate investor offers a much higher valuation than independent funds. How should the startup weigh it?

Terms and strategic strings may be attached
Consider how it affects other investors and acquirers

choices.answer: Weigh less dilution against a high next-round bar and attached strings
distractors: Accept immediately, since higher valuations have no downside
Reject it, since corporate money is never allowed
Ignore the terms, since only the valuation matters

technical.prompt: Why do many corporate venture programmes struggle to last?
expectedPoints: Changes in parent leadership or strategy

choices.answer: Shifting parent priorities, budget cuts and unclear goals
distractors: They are banned from investing for more than five years

technical.prompt: Why should commercial agreements with a portfolio startup be on arm's-length terms?

choices.answer: It keeps the relationship fair and shows genuine traction
distractors: It lets the parent pay nothing
It is required for tax refunds

technical.prompt: Why can marking venture investments to recent rounds make a corporation's earnings volatile?

Corporates must sell stakes every quarter
Accounting rules forbid any gains

choices.answer: Inside information and fairness to other holders need an independent process
distractors: There are no issues because the parent already knows the startup

technical.prompt: How can a corporation attract and keep strong venture investors?

technical.prompt: What do independent venture funds want from a corporate co-investor?

choices.answer: It ignores real strategic benefits to the parent
distractors: IRR always overstates corporate returns
